data.note: 2026-08-19 16:01 - CORRECTION to the previous note: there is NO tk bug. 'tk update <id> --blocked-by <other>' fails loudly and correctly — 'Error: unknown flag: --blocked-by', exit 2, tick untouched — because --blocked-by is registered only on createCmd. My earlier 'silent no-op' claim was an artefact of my own shell hygiene: I piped the command through '2>&1 | tail -1', which discarded the error and the exit code and left a blank line that I read as success. Do not promote the previous note to learnings. The real, transferable lesson is the orchestration one: never pipe a tracker-mutating command through head/tail — you throw away exactly the diagnostics that tell you the mutation did not happen. Check exit status explicitly, and verify the mutation by re-reading state.

1. Doppler is an OPTIONAL rung, never a dependency — see the new .tick/config.md Rule. Offer it when the doppler CLI is present and scoped; otherwise env -> ~/.ticksrc (0600) -> interactive prompt, with no degraded outcome and no error naming a tool the user does not have.

4. wrangler CANNOT mint Cloudflare API tokens (only login/secret/secrets-store). The 'cf' CLI (v0.6.0) CAN: 'cf accounts tokens create' supports --name, --expires-on, --not-before, --condition-request-ip-in/not-in, --dry-run and --body, minting ACCOUNT-OWNED tokens (not user-owned) — scoped to the account, not tied to a person, individually revocable. Bootstrapping it still needs one credential carrying API-Tokens:Edit, which a default cf OAuth profile does NOT have (verified: 87 scopes, zero token-management scopes, 'cf accounts tokens list' -> 403 [9109]).
5. Therefore the credential walk must treat token minting as an OPTIONAL accelerator behind a functional probe ('cf accounts tokens list' succeeds?), never a required step, and must work end to end for an operator who only pastes a token from the dashboard.

data.note:
2026-08-19 17:16 - GATE FAILURE after merge — the live deploy still fails from the repo root, and the cause is a false-positive probe, not the candidate list.

Reproduced in-process: findWrangler resolves to 'npx --no wrangler' and probeVersion returns SUCCESS with version '11.13.0'. That is npm's version, not wrangler's (wrangler is 4.124.0). 'npx --no wrangler --version' exits 0 and prints npx's own version even when no wrangler is installed, so the npx candidate is accepted before the repo-local candidate is ever tried, and the deploy then dies at requireAuth with 'a logged-in wrangler is required'.

This is the repo's own documented green-start trap one layer down: a cleanly-succeeding probe that did no work. probeVersion trusts an exit code and never checks WHAT answered.

Fix: probeVersion must verify the responder is actually wrangler — assert the '--version' output identifies wrangler (and/or parse a plausible wrangler version) and reject the candidate otherwise, so resolution falls through to the next one. Add a regression test with a fake npx-shaped binary that exits 0 and prints an unrelated version: resolution must skip it and land on the repo-local wrangler.

Verified facts for the fix: the repo-local candidate itself is fine — /Users/.../cloud/factory/node_modules/.bin/wrangler --version prints 4.124.0 and whoami exits 0 from both the repo root and the staged bundle dir. Only the ordering plus the unvalidated npx probe is wrong.

The only failure is TestDeployResolvesWranglerThroughNpx (deploy_test.go:516), and it is a path-ordering bug introduced by the new chdir guard, not a regression in the resolver:

  restore := chdir(t, t.TempDir())                                   // line ~488 — cwd is now a temp dir
  fakeNpx, _ := filepath.Abs(filepath.Join("testdata", "fake-npx.sh"))  // line ~493 — resolves against the TEMP dir

Because the abs paths are computed AFTER the chdir, 'testdata/fake-npx.sh' resolves to <tmpdir>/testdata/fake-npx.sh, which does not exist. The symlinks are therefore dangling, npx cannot exec, every candidate fails, and Deploy returns the 'wrangler is required' PrerequisiteError.

Fix: resolve both filepath.Abs(...) values BEFORE the chdir (or capture the package dir first and join against it). The chdir guard itself is right and should stay — it is what stops the repo's own dependency from winning in a checkout.

data.note:
2026-08-19 18:23 - Design guidance (human question, 2026-08-19): the same image runs many times per repo with fresh clones — do NOT let that imply per-task image builds.

Layering:
1. BASE IMAGE, pinned to the tk version (same cadence as the factory bundle, which tk factory deploy already version-pins): git, the harness CLIs, language runtimes. Built and pushed at deploy time, instantiated per run. Starting the Nth container costs no rebuild.
2. REPO DEPENDENCY CACHE — persisted, never baked into the image. Baking node_modules means rebuilding the image on every lockfile change, which is the treadmill this question is trying to avoid. Prefer a named sandbox per project whose filesystem survives sleep/wake (pnpm store, ~/.cache/go-build, ~/.cargo), so a fresh clone lands in a warm container. Snapshot/restore is the alternative.

HARD CONSTRAINT (axiom 1): cache warmth is convenience state. A cold sandbox with an empty cache must always produce a CORRECT run — warmth buys speed, never correctness. Never let a green build depend on a warm worker. Verify the actual Sandbox persistence/snapshot API rather than assuming it; this epic already paid once for assuming a platform behaviour (the PBKDF2 cap).

Related gap, flagged not assigned: .tick/config.md has an Environment section, but it is VERIFICATION only (test, don't ask). There is no place to declare how to WARM a repo (pnpm install --frozen-lockfile in cloud/factory, go mod download). A 'Setup' section — idempotent, cache-populating commands — would give this entrypoint something to run and would help local runs too. If you think it belongs in this tick, say so in your report rather than adding it silently.
data.title: Orchestrator sandbox image and headless harness bootstrap

data.note:
2026-08-19 18:26 - Scope addition (human decision, 2026-08-19): ONE factory serves MANY projects. Two consequences this tick owns:

1. PROJECT ENROLLMENT IS REQUIRED. Today nothing restricts which repo a run may be submitted for — the bearer token is the only gate, so any token holder could submit any owner/repo and the factory would clone and run it. Add an enrolled-projects table (D1) and reject a submission for an unenrolled project with an actionable error naming the enrolment command. Enrolment records owner/repo plus the credential grade it may use. This is a security boundary, not bookkeeping: it is what stops a leaked token from turning the factory into an arbitrary-code runner for any repo on GitHub.
2. PROJECT IS A FIRST-CLASS KEY EVERYWHERE. The lease is per project (RunRoom idFromName(project+epic)), so two repos run concurrently without contending; runs/signals/dispatch_log all carry project; R2 keys carry it. Do not let any route assume a single implicit project.

Explicitly NOT in scope: parameterising the worker/D1/R2 resource names. One factory per Cloudflare account is the intended constraint (see the design doc), so the fixed names ticks-factory / ticks-factory-artifacts are correct — they just need to be a stated constraint rather than an accident.

data.note:
2026-08-19 18:28 - Design correction + constraint (human question, 2026-08-19). My earlier note said the image is 'built and pushed once at tk factory deploy' — too absolute. The real question is where PER-REPO TOOLCHAIN provisioning happens, and it is now a hard constraint rather than a preference:

The epic has just documented 'one factory, many projects — adding a repo is ENROLMENT, not deployment'. If enrolling a repo required building and pushing a container image, that statement is false. So the image design must make adding a repo cost ZERO image work.

Rejected: a per-repo image (enrolment becomes a build, and N images must each stay pinned to the tk version). Also rejected as the primary answer: a fat base image carrying every runtime — cold starts are per-tick in Phase 2, so image size is a recurring cost, and it is always eventually missing a toolchain, at which point every project pays for a rebuild.

Preferred: THIN BASE + PROVISIONED TOOLCHAIN. Base carries git, the harness CLIs and a version manager (mise/asdf-class) — nothing repo-specific, rebuilt only when tk or a harness version changes. The entrypoint provisions the repo's declared toolchain on first run for that project, landing in the project's persistent sandbox so it is warm from run two onward — the same cache mechanism as dependencies. Adding Rust support then becomes a line in one repo's config, not a factory-wide rebuild.

Toolchain declaration source: prefer the ecosystem's own pins (go.mod, package.json, .tool-versions) over inventing a format. .tick/config.md Environment is VERIFICATION only, so it cannot serve here — same gap as the missing Setup section.

Escape hatch: a repo may pin a custom image explicitly, opt-in, for genuinely exotic needs.

Unchanged: axiom 1 — first run cold and slow is fine, every later run warm; a cold sandbox with an empty cache must still produce a CORRECT run.
data.title: Orchestrator sandbox image and headless harness bootstrap

data.note:
2026-08-19 18:29 - [human] REVISION (human decision, 2026-08-19) — supersedes my previous note's rejection of a batteries-included base image.

The operator wants ONE image spec'd to cover ~99% of their projects. That decision stands and my previous guidance was over-generalised: 'thin base + provision everything' is the right default for a general-purpose tool, not for a single-operator factory with a known project mix.

BUILD: a batteries-included base image carrying the declared common set — Node/TypeScript with pnpm, Python with uv, Go, plus git, ripgrep, jq and a C build toolchain — alongside the harness CLIs. Pinned to the tk version, rebuilt only when tk, a harness, or the declared toolchain set changes.

KEEP the version manager (mise/asdf-class) in the image anyway, as the ESCAPE HATCH rather than the primary path. Then the 99% costs nothing at run time, and a repo needing something outside the set (Rust, say) provisions it on first run into the project's persistent sandbox instead of forcing a factory-wide rebuild. This is what preserves the documented rule that adding a repo is ENROLMENT, not deployment, without requiring the operator to predict every toolchain up front.

STATE THE COST HONESTLY IN THE REPORT: image size is paid on cold start, and Phase 2 starts a container per tick, so a ~2GB image across five parallel workers is real wall-clock. Note the mitigation (named sandboxes that sleep/wake rather than cold-start, so the image is already pulled) and keep CACHES out of the image — runtimes belong in the image, dependency caches belong in the persistent sandbox.

Unchanged: axiom 1 — a cold sandbox with an empty cache must still produce a correct run.

2. FREE-TEXT ANSWERS ARE AMBIGUOUS, and this is a correctness issue rather than a nicety. Rules to implement, fail-closed:
   - A Telegram reply-to a specific question message resolves THAT question. Deterministic; prefer it.
   - Bare text with exactly ONE open question across all projects resolves it.
   - Bare text with TWO OR MORE open questions must REFUSE and list the candidates. Never guess: an approval carries human provenance into the verdict guard, so a wrong guess attributes the operator's approval to another project's gate.

3. UPGRADE PATH, optional: a Telegram supergroup in forum mode gives one topic per project via message_thread_id — one bot, one chat, natively separate threads, replies scoped to their topic. data.note:
2026-08-19 21:40 - [human] Telegram Topics mechanics (human confirmed topics are the right answer, 2026-08-19):
- 'Topics' in the UI IS 'forum' in the Bot API (is_forum on the chat). Same feature, two names — there is no separate forum object to create. The operator already runs Topics in another group, so the capability is proven on their account.
- Requires a supergroup; enabling Topics upgrades a basic group automatically. The bot must be a member; it needs can_manage_topics ONLY to create topics itself. Posting into an existing topic just needs message_thread_id on sendMessage.
- CONFIG SHAPE CHANGE: the current channel config is a private chat (operator.json has user_id == chat_id). Group + topics means a new chat_id plus a per-project message_thread_id map. Design that map as part of project enrolment, not as a fourth config surface.
- BOT PRIVACY MODE is the non-obvious trap: in groups a bot sees only commands and REPLIES TO ITS OWN MESSAGES by default, not general chatter. Recommendation: keep privacy mode ON and rely on reply-to plus inline buttons (callbacks always reach the bot regardless). Consequence: in a group the reply-to convention stops being a nicety and becomes load-bearing for free-text answers — the fail-closed rules already recorded here still apply, but the common path becomes reply-scoped and therefore unambiguous by construction. Disabling privacy mode would let the bot read every message in a group the operator also uses for other things; that is a larger surface than this needs.
- Verification when implementing: getChat on the target group and assert is_forum, and getMe/getChatMember to confirm the bot's rights, rather than assuming — the operator's account already has a working example to test against.

- NO MID-RUN MUTATION PATH (D21) — PASS, verified by absence: no steer/inject/prompt/message route exists on the run API. Steering is stop, edit the tracker, run again.
- PRE-FLIGHT — PASS after orl: zero markdown parsing left in preflight.sh; the entrypoint asks the verified tk binary, so a migrated repo actually runs its checks instead of silently passing.

FINDING 1 — SHOULD-FIX (high confidence). A run whose gateway cost telemetry is unavailable still STARTS, bounded only by wall clock, with the fact logged and recorded (run-workflow.ts acquireContext: 'Reported, not enforced'). The reasoning is sound as far as it goes — a telemetry outage should not take the factory down, and recording 'cost unknown' beats implying zero spend. But the consequence is that an explicitly configured cost budget silently degrades to wall-clock-only, which is the one budget an operator sets precisely because wall clock does not bound spend on metered keys. Recommend: when a cost budget is explicitly configured and telemetry cannot be read, REFUSE the run with an actionable message; proceed only when no cost budget was set. That keeps the outage-tolerance for the common case and preserves the guarantee for the operator who asked for one.

No blockers. This epic's real defects were all caught earlier by the gate, the foundation review, and live deployment — which is the finding worth carrying into the retro.

data.note:
2026-08-20 14:38 - [human] SCOPE CORRECTION (operator, 2026-08-20) — read before going further; this narrows the tick.

The operator's framing is better than the one this tick was written with: the question is not 'where is the orchestrator' but 'what is available here', and ticks ALREADY has that mechanism — substrate = "auto" probes for herdr and falls back to harness silently when absent. The motivating scenario is a repo sometimes driven through herdr and sometimes through the cloud factory, which is exactly what auto is for.

So the real defect is narrower than this description implies: THIS REPO PINS substrate = "herdr", a hard assertion that herdr is always reachable. True on a laptop, false in a container. With auto, the first cloud run would have probed, found no socket, and degraded — no new mechanism required.

Evaluate and choose, saying which and why in the report:
A. auto is the answer and the pin was the bug. Set this repo to auto, and reduce this tick to documentation plus (maybe) a clear failure when an explicit herdr pin is unsatisfiable. Uses what exists; adds no vocabulary.
B. an explicit signal is still warranted for what CANNOT be probed. auto answers 'is herdr reachable', not 'should I use it' — a cloud sandbox might one day have a reachable socket (herdr-in-the-cloud is a documented open door) and still want harness. And [orchestration].max_parallel has no probe at all: a laptop's 3 should not govern a container.

My reading is A for substrate, B only for the unprobeable keys — do not add an env var that duplicates what auto already decides. If you land B for anything, it must be a THIN override consulted by the existing resolution path (eb5's internal/sandbox/substrate.go), never a parallel mechanism.

Also check: does the existing explicit-degradation announcement fire on the auto path? The protocol requires a degraded substrate to be stated and noted; if auto is silent by design (the code comments suggest auto/unavailable is), a cloud run falling back to harness would do so invisibly, which is its own small problem worth naming.
data.title: Explicit orchestrator-location signal (TICKS_ORCHESTRATOR), not inference

data.note:
2026-08-20 14:39 - [human] Third case from the operator, and it settles the argument for A. The same repo is operated three ways:
  1. local Claude Code + herdr panes            -> substrate herdr
  2. local Claude Code, NO herdr, Claude subagents -> substrate harness   (the skill's ORIGINAL mode, predating herdr)
  3. cloud orchestrator, subagents in one container -> substrate harness

Cases 2 and 3 are the SAME situation — no herdr available — reached from different directions, which is precisely what auto resolves. An env var keyed on 'am I in the cloud' would fix case 3 and leave case 2 broken, so it is the wrong axis.

Note what the current pin does to case 2 TODAY, on this repo: a local Claude session with no herdr running hits the explicit-degradation path. It still works, but it announces a degradation and notes it on every run, when the truthful configuration is 'use herdr when it is there'. That is the pin being wrong, not the fallback being wrong.

The design doc backs this: the fully local, no-herdr, no-cloud path is called the degenerate case that must stay sacred and work offline forever. A pin that makes it announce a failure every time is not honouring that.

So: set this repo to auto, and make sure the announcement distinguishes 'you asked for herdr and could not have it' (worth saying loudly) from 'auto found no herdr and used subagents' (normal, worth saying quietly once, not as a degradation). If the current code cannot tell those apart, that is the thing to fix.

data.note:
2026-08-20 14:40 - [human] FINAL narrowing (operator, 2026-08-20). The local case is not one thing — it is claude, codex, pi or prime, each with or without herdr. That is the TWO-AXIS model the skill already documents, and the env var I originally specified collapsed it into one:

              herdr substrate        harness substrate
  Claude Code herdr panes            Claude subagents
  Codex       herdr panes            codex subagents
  Pi          herdr panes            Pi's own dispatch
  Prime       herdr panes            Prime's dispatch
  cloud       (open door, not P1)    subagents in one container

Both axes already resolve themselves, independently and correctly:
- HARNESS by capability probe, and agent-runner.md is emphatic that it must be detected from runtime capabilities rather than the system prompt's self-description (Prime opens with a Claude-Code-style preamble while being a different runtime), and RE-DETECTED every session because adapter choice is per-session state a tracker note cannot carry.
- SUBSTRATE by auto probing for herdr.

So TICKS_ORCHESTRATOR=local|cloud was wrong twice: it would have to enumerate a product-by-location matrix that keeps growing, and neither axis needs telling because both are probed.

What is genuinely UN-PROBEABLE is only this, and it is all that may justify any new configuration:
1. orchestration.max_parallel — a laptop's 3 is not a container's 3, and nothing probes it.
2. 'herdr is reachable but should not be used' — hypothetical until herdr-in-the-cloud exists; do not build for it now.

Recommendation stands and is now firmer: set this repo to auto, fix the loud-vs-quiet announcement distinction, and add NO location vocabulary. If max_parallel needs a cloud-appropriate value, prefer deriving it from what the sandbox can actually support over adding an env var that means 'I am in the cloud'.

2026-08-20 14:41 - [human] Third axis (operator, 2026-08-20), and it is the one my env var confused worst. There are THREE independent things:
  1. ORCHESTRATOR HARNESS  — who drives the loop (claude | codex | pi | prime) — settled by capability probe, re-detected per session.
  2. ORCHESTRATOR LOCATION — laptop or container — settled by NOTHING, because nothing needs it. That was my error.
  3. WORKER SUBSTRATE      — how workers are dispatched (harness | herdr | cloud) — settled by auto probing.

D19 states 1/2 and 3 are ORTHOGONAL, and the matrix in the design doc is explicit:
    Orchestrator / Workers    harness    herdr    cloud
    Local terminal            today      today    tk cloud spawn/wait/collect/reconcile
    Cloud Workflow            Phase 1    (open)   Phase 2

So 'cloud' is not one thing: it is a value on the WORKER axis (substrate = "cloud", Phase 2 tick bmo) AND separately a place the orchestrator can sit. TICKS_ORCHESTRATOR=cloud would have smeared those together, and would specifically have broken the row the design cares most about — a LOCAL orchestrator driving CLOUD workers ('local judgment, cloud hands'), where the operator keeps orchestrating from their terminal and stops paying for five local worktrees.

Concretely for this tick: a variable meaning 'I am in the cloud' would have to be consulted by BOTH the substrate resolution and whatever dispatches workers, and would give the wrong answer for local-orchestrator-plus-cloud-workers, which is a supported configuration and not a hypothetical. Do not add it.

Nothing changes in the recommendation — auto, plus the loud-vs-quiet announcement fix — but the reason is now three-deep, and the tick description should say why a location signal is the wrong shape so this is not re-proposed later.

data.note:
2026-08-20 14:43 - [human] SYSTEMATIC ENUMERATION (operator asked for it, 2026-08-20). Implement from this table, not from the tick's original prose.

FIVE AXES, not two:
  1 orchestrator harness    claude|codex|pi|prime|(omp)  -> capability probe, per session
  2 orchestrator location   laptop|cloud container       -> NOTHING, and nothing needs it
  3 orchestrator containment inside a herdr pane or not   -> HERDR_ENV=1
  4 worker substrate        harness|herdr|cloud          -> auto probe, or explicit
  5 worker kind (per role)  claude|codex|pi|...          -> [roles.*.kind]

Axis 3 is the one we had not separated: ProbeEnv reports 'I am in a herdr pane' and that is used as evidence herdr is AVAILABLE. Sound as availability evidence; it is NOT a statement about where workers should go. It is a probe input to axis 4, not a configuration axis.

AUTO RESOLUTION, all four in-scope cases:
  laptop, in herdr pane            -> herdr    correct
  laptop, no pane, herdr running   -> herdr    correct
  laptop, no pane, no herdr        -> harness  correct
  cloud container                  -> harness  correct (Phase 1)
auto is right in every case. That is the enumerated proof that no location signal is needed — stronger than the argument I gave before.

THE OPERATOR'S SCENARIO (local harness, in or out of herdr, driving CLOUD workers) works, but only via EXPLICIT substrate = "cloud", never auto, for two structural reasons that are both correct:
  - auto can never resolve to cloud: you cannot probe 'should I spend money in a cloud account'. Cloud is opt-in by construction.
  - inside a herdr pane auto picks herdr, because herdr genuinely IS available. Wanting cloud anyway is an explicit choice, and explicit beats probe.
So axes 3 and 4 are fully independent: in a herdr pane, driving cloud workers, is substrate = cloud with HERDR_ENV=1. Nothing conflicts. NOTE the enum today is auto|harness|herdr — cloud does not exist yet (Phase 2, bmo).

THE ONE REAL DEFECT IN SCOPE FOR THIS TICK — the announcement matrix. Per substrate.go's own comment, only explicit-herdr-unavailable produces text; auto/available and auto/unavailable are both SILENT. Silence is right on a laptop (normal) and wrong in the cloud (you cannot tell from the log why harness was chosen, or whether it was deliberate), and it is the SAME silence either way so the two cannot be distinguished.
Fix: state the resolved substrate once, always, quietly — including on the auto path — and keep 'you asked for herdr and cannot have it' loud. That is not a location concern; it is just saying what you resolved.

data.note:
2026-08-20 14:57 - ORCHESTRATION DEFECT, operator-caught twice (2026-08-20). Workers finished and the orchestrator did not notice.

Mechanism: the real 'tk herd wait' is run detached (nohup + disown) so it survives, and a SEPARATE harness-backgrounded poller watches its output file to produce a completion notification. When the operator interrupts with a question, the poller is not re-established afterwards. The detached wait still completes and writes its file — nothing reads it. So the wait is fine; the NOTIFICATION is what breaks, and it breaks precisely during operator conversation, which is when the orchestrator is least likely to notice on its own.

Both times this happened, it followed a run of design questions. Answering them is correct; dropping the loop is not.

RULE: check worker state at the START of every turn, unconditionally — one 'herdr agent list' plus 'tk herd collect --epic <id>' — rather than relying on a notification arriving. Cheap, and immune to interruption. A settled worker is discovered by looking, not by being told.

This belongs in the skill, not just here: the herdr adapter documents wait discipline as event-driven fan-in, which is right for the WAIT, but says nothing about an orchestrator that is also having a conversation. An orchestrator with a human in the loop must poll its own workers at turn boundaries.

2026-08-20 17:39 - [human] CORRECTION (operator, 2026-08-20): my earlier note put kimi-k2.7-code and qwen2.5-coder-32b-instruct forward as the code-specialised candidates. Both are a generation behind — qwen2.5-coder predates qwen3.8, and the kimi entries predate the current families. The leading Cloudflare-hosted candidates are DEEPSEEK V4 (pro-0813 / flash-0731) and QWEN 3.8 (qwen3.8-27b). Compare those; treat the older coder-tagged models as baselines at most.

DEEPSWE RESEARCH (together.ai/blog/deepswe; agentica-org/DeepSWE-Preview), and what it implies for OUR choice — DeepSWE is a coding agent trained from Qwen3-32B with pure RL: 42.2% Pass@1 on SWE-Bench-Verified, 59% with K=16 test-time scaling, +20 points from 200 RL steps.
  1. REASONING MODE MATTERS. Non-thinking mode gave 'limited performance improvement'. deepseek-v4-pro emits reasoning_content — it is a thinking model, which the research says is the property that counts for this domain. Check whether qwen3.8-27b exposes the same.
  2. CONTEXT LENGTH IS NOT THE LEVER. 16K -> 128K bought <=2%. Directly relevant to our cost: the live run re-sends ~77-79k input tokens EVERY turn (900k input tokens across 16 calls, $1.17 in seven minutes). If context is not buying capability, that spend is mostly waste and the orchestrator prompt/context strategy is worth attacking before the model choice is.
  3. DELIBERATE SUBMISSION. DeepSWE masks trajectories that hit max context, max steps or timeout, rewarding only deliberate submission — 'ensuring reward is only assigned when an agent deliberately submits encourages rigorous testing'. That is exactly the principle behind tick ehy: a run whose harness stops without durable evidence is not complete. Convergent, and worth stating in the recommendation.
  4. RL POST-TRAINING BEATS SCALE OR DISTILLATION. Pure RL from Qwen3-32B beat distilling from stronger proprietary models. So the selection question is which candidate has AGENTIC post-training, not which is largest.
  5. TRAJECTORY MULTIPLICITY over token scaling; most gains by K=8. Not applicable to a single orchestrator, but relevant if implementers are ever run as competing attempts.

LIVE EVIDENCE, which outranks any benchmark for the orchestrator role: gpt-oss-120b made ONE call and stopped. deepseek-v4-pro has sustained 16+ calls with real bash tool_calls and coherent reasoning about base branch, detached HEAD and the repo's PR+CI rule. Same prompt, same substrate, same probes — only the model changed.

data.note:
2026-08-21 10:15 - RETRO ADDENDUM — the four P0s found by running the thing for real (2026-08-21)

Phase 1 shipped a control plane that was correct up to the credential boundary. Then one real run
of epic 72y — 892 calls, 4.4 hours, seven ticks implemented — exposed four defects that every green
suite had missed, and lost all seven ticks. Each is now closed:

- cts: the cost query trusted result_info.total_pages, a field the gateway logs API does not send.
  Defaulted to 1, stopped after 50 of 892 entries, reported $2.98 against a real $49.80 and a $25
  ceiling. A budget fed by a truncated query is not a budget.
- gyl: the kill switch was decorative — NOT because the per-request revocation check was wrong (it
  was right, and tested) but because supervisePass minted a fresh token at every boot, and closeout
  ran with enforce_budgets:false so it read no stop record at all. Only container deletion stopped
  the run. Durability is now a refusal to MINT, checked before every boot.
- tpl: nothing reached origin until closeout, so the seven implemented ticks died with the
  container. Now a keeper loop pushes tick-run/<epic> on a timer, from the container, mechanically.
- l8z: 46M input tokens at zero cache hits. Workers AI prefix caching needs x-session-affinity,
  which the gateway never set. Now stamped from the run id, with the injected prompt pinned
  byte-identical so one varying token cannot invalidate the prefix.

Plus fw6, filed from a billing audit rather than a failure: the factory could route to anthropic,
openai or openrouter, and the only thing preventing cash spend was the ABSENCE of a vendor key.
Now workers-ai is the sole default route and the refusal states the billing consequence.

THE PATTERN. Every one of these is the green-start trap in a new costume: a permissive default
(total_pages -> 1), a check that something else undoes (revoke -> re-mint), an absence mistaken for
a guarantee (no vendor key -> no cash route), and a header nobody set (no affinity -> no caching).
The suites were green because each was internally consistent. What caught them was spending real
money for four hours. Phase 2's benchmarking tick (kuf) is the deliberate version of that.

BILLING, now confirmed on the operator dashboard rather than assumed: Workers AI is credit-covered
(Startup Program caps Workers AI at $50k, R2 at $10k); AI Gateway is excluded. Cloudflare classifies
gateway-routed Workers AI as Workers AI — 4.54M Neurons on deepseek-v4-pro, matching the gateway
log's dollar figure. Mid-cycle billable usage showed none of it, which is lag, not absence. Two
follow-ups filed on 1vn: h4n (assert postpaid billing mode) and wn5 (per-run budget flags).

CEILINGS. RUN_MAX_COST_USD 25 -> 5 and RUN_MAX_WALL_CLOCK_MS 6h -> 45m, deliberately small until a
run is measured with enforcement that works. These are safety numbers, not capacity numbers; raise
them from measurement, not from a stalled run.

data.note: 2026-08-21 18:05 - HYPOTHESIS REFUTED BY MEASUREMENT — the orchestrator's suspicion (mine) was wrong on every count, and the numbers are worth keeping. Clustering all 230 calls of run_62c289d1 by conversation found 8 conversations (1 orchestrator, 7 implementers). Concurrency HELPS rather than interferes: 67.9 percent cached during fan-out with 6+ conversations live against 52.4 percent while the orchestrator ran alone, and a call whose predecessor was a DIFFERENT conversation cached better (65.7) than one following its own (62.4). Interference would show the opposite sign. The bytes did not vary either: call 12's entire 220,891-char body is a byte-exact prefix of call 13's, same tools hash, and call 13 was still billed 512 cached of 74,605. Controlled probes gave noise in both directions. Affinity is not stickiness at all — a single conversation alone on its own key still cached 0 percent on two of three follow-ups. Caching warms up: the first repeat of a prefix always bills 0. And a miss is a floor rather than a zero — calls are billed a cached count equal to an early snapshot of that conversation, i.e. they reached an instance that saw it once and never since. The misses are instance-side, so the key stays per run.
data.title: One session-affinity key for N concurrent subagents may defeat prefix caching

data.note:
2026-08-23 06:51 - PHASE 2 RETRO (closeout ihf, 2026-08-23).

WHAT PHASE 2 DELIVERED. A cloud run dispatches one worker CONTAINER per tick; each boots on a Workers AI model through the factory gateway, does real work, pushes a branch and a report; the in-run orchestrator collects and merges them onto the run branch with no local orchestrator in the loop. Proven live on run_659b7cf253e4462aa6c0dfebbe820ddd — three containers, three branches with real implementation commits, clean boundaries, zero exit-7 boots.

THE SHAPE OF THE EPIC, and it is the finding that matters most. Phase 2's code was declared correct by tick oun's final review with 216 vitest cases and the full Go suite green. Everything in the list below was invisible to all of it, and every one was found by RUNNING the thing:

  ys3  workers resolved the repo's [roles.implement] (an anthropic model) against a Workers-AI-only
       gateway. Exit 7, every worker, every wave. Seven paid runs of misdiagnosis.
  2xm  the dispatch step blocked past Cloudflare's 10-minute step cap, so every run killed its own
       supervisor while the run record still said 'running'. This hid behind ys3.
  5fg  the worker harness budget was a 30-minute constant that ignored --max-wall-clock, with a
       second 45-minute clamp underneath it.
  dxk  a worker committed tracker state although its prompt forbade it in as many words.
  1cd  the worker model was a hardcoded constant, and the model it named finished 1 of 3 real ticks.
  7zk  a budget trip destroyed three working containers and kept nothing. $8 for zero output.
  7n7  the lease TTL is 10 minutes and a container wave runs 60-90, so the wave-2 pass always found
       a lapsed lease and hard-stopped 15 seconds after boot.
  0fg  a worker container's own output went nowhere, which is why ys3 cost seven runs and not one.
  3gr  a worker that succeeded without writing a report was told to re-dispatch — advice to pay to
       redo finished work.
  kya, 4qx, 6uv, wiy  found by review or by reading the code that the runs pointed at.

Twelve defects. Not one was a logic error the suite could have caught; every one was an assumption about a boundary — a platform limit, a credential scope, a config cell read by two runtimes, a model's willingness to follow instructions.

THE METHOD LESSON, paid for at roughly seven runs and $4 before it was learned. Six runs were diagnosed by INFERENCE from a log never built to answer the question. The seventh persisted what the call actually RETURNED and answered it immediately. The generalisation is now in .tick/learnings.md: a log holds what you believed, the return value is evidence. Its twin, learned two defects later: a supervisor cannot report its own death, because the record is written by the thing that may be gone — read the Workflow instance, not the run record.

COST. Seven live runs, ~$45 total. deepseek-v4-flash: 94-99% prompt cache, ~$0.6-1.4 per three-container run, and 1 of 3 real ticks finished. deepseek-v4-pro: ~$10-12 per run, 3 of 3. Cost per COMPLETED tick is the only ranking that survived contact — a model that does not converge costs 100% of its tokens for 0% of the work.

WHAT I WOULD DO DIFFERENTLY. Instrument the return value BEFORE the first live run, not after the seventh. The instrumentation ys3 added cost one tick and would have saved six runs; the per-worker log stream 0fg added cost one tick and turned the eventual diagnosis into a three-minute read. On a paid substrate, observability is not a follow-up — it is the first tick.

Partitioning notes, so a re-planner does not undo them on purpose:
- 8sm carries external_ref dedup even though dedup 'belongs' to each source. One implementation, not three — the sources all redeliver.
- spq bundles webhook mode with project legibility because both rewrite message composition; separating them guarantees a merge conflict for no benefit.
- 0vb (generic webhook sources) is deliberately AFTER vuz (GitHub). The concrete source teaches what the generic registration needs, and this repo has already paid once for a config surface designed before its first consumer.
- yu8 is P0 despite reading like UX. A wrong guess at which question a bare answer resolves does not answer the wrong question, it forges the operator's consent into another project's gate.

FOUR PHASE 2 CARRY-FORWARDS, NOT ADDED HERE — placing them is a human roadmap decision, so they are recorded rather than filed:

1. PER-TICK TIER SELECTION ON THE CLOUD SUBSTRATE. [roles.implement].tiers expresses it for local workers; the cloud path has none, so every container gets one model whether the tick is a one-line fix or a TUI rewrite. Measured: deepseek-v4-flash finished 1 of 3 real ticks, v4-pro 3 of 3 at ~8x the cost. Tiering is what makes the cheap rung pay again. This is the highest-value of the four.
2. FAN-OUT CEILING IS 3, NOT 6. [[containers]] max_instances = 3 in wrangler.toml caps concurrency below [orchestration].max_parallel. Tick kuf's N=5 degradation curve cannot be reproduced until it moves.
3. WORKER HARNESS OUTPUT DOES NOT STREAM. Tick 0fg streams a container's BOOT reliably — which is what made the exit-7 diagnosis instant — but everything after 'starting the omp harness' never reaches R2. Diagnosing a mid-run stall still needs the gateway trace.
4. A SUPERVISOR'S DEATH IS INVISIBLE. Tick 2xm fixed the cause (the 10-minute step cap) but not the class: the run record is written by the thing that may be gone, so a dead supervisor still reads as 'running'. A liveness signal observable from outside the supervisor is the general fix.

All four are in repo-wiki/phase-2-live-verification.md with the evidence.

data.reason: Completed: the signal funnel. submitSignal() validates and hands to a per-project Durable Object (idFromName(project), as the RunRoom is addressed) that assigns a monotonic seq and commits in that order. Two independent defences, only one of which is the queue: the write path is CREATE-ONLY, so a signal can only ever add a file and never replace one, and the contents API is a compare-and-swap on the branch ref so a concurrent run-commit fails the write with 409 having changed nothing. Nothing in Phase 3 blew up in production, and the reason is not that this code is better — it is that Phase 3 had Phase 2's list of boundary classes to check against: platform limits, credential scope, shared config cells, untrusted input, and a supervisor that cannot report its own death. data.note:
2026-08-24 21:44 - PHASE 4 RETRO (closeout 7xe, 2026-08-24).

WHAT PHASE 4 DELIVERED. Three loops that run without being asked — CI-failure remediation on factory-owned branches, read-only PR review, and cron sweeps — plus the two things that make autonomy survivable: a credential grade that cannot be self-selected, and a way to find out when a loop fails while nobody was watching.

THE PATTERN ACROSS THREE EPICS, and it is the most useful thing this retro can record:
  Phase 2  twelve defects, all found by RUNNING it. Nothing else could have.
  Phase 3  five defects, found by REVIEWING against Phase 2's list of boundary classes.
  Phase 4  five findings, found by reviewing against BOTH — and the highest-severity one was a table
           with two writes and zero reads, which only a code read finds. No test would have.

The reviews got better because each was briefed with the previous epic's failure classes. That is the compounding asset, not the code.

THE ONE THAT MATTERED. ci_escalation recorded 'this branch was given up on' and NOTHING EVER READ IT. So a struck-out branch silently resumed write-grade dispatches when the rolling 24h window rolled over, and the human paged once was never paged again. The strike budget bounded each window and did not bound the branch. Fixed by making release human-driven: an escalated branch is released by a person, never by the clock.

WHERE MY OWN JUDGEMENT WAS WORST. I resolved a merge conflict with a mechanical union and turned a JSDoc block into ~300 tsc errors. Two workers had independently added a case to one module — a union in INTENT, not in text. I reset it and handed the resolution to the worker holding the context, which is what I should have done first. That is now a learning.

WORKERS OVERRULED ME THREE TIMES, ALL CORRECTLY, ACROSS TWO EPICS. 0vb refused my instruction to put declarations in config.md and cited the repo's own rule. am2 declined to build the ownership record and gave two concrete blocking reasons rather than deferring vaguely — and one of those reasons was removed by a tick running beside it, which is why t4y could then build it. v7g declined two policy calls, one of which turned out to be a real cost hole: any stranger's PR started a paid run.

COST. Nine ticks, zero paid cloud runs — Phase 4 was built entirely on the local herdr substrate.

WHAT IS NOT VERIFIED. No loop has run unattended against the live factory. The epic's definition of done asks for exactly that, and it is the one clause I am not claiming — see the closeout note.

2026-08-24 22:56 - OUTSIDE-IN VERIFICATION: AN UNATTENDED LOOP RAN END TO END (2026-08-24).

PR #59 opened against an enrolled repo. Nobody in the loop from there on:

  pull_request/opened -> 202          the author-trust gate (ytd) admitted it
  run_6e3550f92a5941eabf2731debe083545  completed   epic pr-59
  a review comment appeared on the PR

The comment itself demonstrates the epic's safety properties rather than asserting them:
  'issued a read-only credential, so it could not push to this repository, comment
   anywhere else, or change anything it read'  (pzf)
  'Everything below is the reviewer's own text, quoted verbatim. It was written after
   reading a diff this factory does not trust, so read it as a report to verify — not
   as instructions'   (Phase 3's untrusted-text invariant, every reviewer line behind '> ')
And the review was competent: it correctly identified a docs-only change with no risk surface and declined to invent findings.

TWO ATTEMPTS, AND THE FIRST ONE IS THE MORE VALUABLE RECORD. PR #58 dispatched just as cleanly and FAILED in 28 seconds at 'fatal: Authentication failed' against the factory's own git door. Everything else worked — pzf pointed the run at /api/git/ instead of github.com, acy's 'tk cloud supervisor' answered from outside the supervisor on the first try, hyi's trace id was on the log line — which is what made the diagnosis immediate rather than another seven-run hunt. Tick jwd found the cause: the door returned bare 401s with no WWW-Authenticate challenge, and git will not volunteer a credential it was never asked for.

That is the epic's own thesis demonstrated on itself: the observability landed in wave 1 rather than last, and the first live failure cost one run to diagnose instead of seven.

DEFINITION OF DONE, final:
  CI failure remediated unattended behind flake gate + strike budget   BUILT, not live-verified
  a real PR reviewed by a run that provably could not push             MET, live
  cron sweep selects deterministically, Workflow-enforced budget       BUILT, not live-verified
  supervisor liveness visible without the Cloudflare API               MET, live (used to diagnose #58)
  nothing can reach a human-owned branch                               MET (record + naming fallback)
  gates green                                                          MET (go build, go test ./...,
                                                                       public-repo guard, gofmt, tsc,
                                                                       factory vitest 1184)

Two clauses are BUILT AND TESTED BUT NOT LIVE-VERIFIED: CI remediation needs a real failing check on a factory-owned branch, and a cron sweep needs a schedule to fire. Both are recorded as not-claimed rather than glossed — the PR review loop was chosen for the live check because it is the safest of the three, which was the sequencing argument for building it first.

That evidence is now in protocol.go, and it is what the forward-compatible policy rests on — recorded as one dated observation against one version, not a guarantee, which is why the floor stays a hard stop. A worker container has no keeper, so a sandbox sleep wipes its work unrecoverably

data.note:
2026-08-25 14:19 - CORRECTION (2026-08-25), to the RUN 2 VERDICT recorded above.

I wrote that run_9e40b9563bfb493cac1fe6625356e538's workers 'went on working orphaned until 14:02, and nothing collected them'. Orphaned-but-alive is probably wrong. They were most likely SLEPT AND WIPED by the platform.

Cloudflare stops a sandbox after sleepAfter and the filesystem does not survive — 'all previous state is lost'. SANDBOX_SLEEP_AFTER is 20m, and the supervisor's polling is what keeps a sandbox awake. That supervisor died at ~13:32. The workers' last model call was 14:02, about twenty minutes later. Then nothing.

The detail that decides it: those workers produced NO FALLBACK REPORT. A container that is merely orphaned but running still reaches worker.sh's tail and writes one — that is what the fallback exists for, and runs 1 and 3 both produced them. Absence of the report means the container never reached its own tail, which is what a platform stop looks like and not what an uncollected-but-alive container looks like.

Filed as tick iu9: the worker container has no keeper, unlike the orchestrator, so it holds everything in its filesystem until it finishes and pushes once. 5fg's salvage and 7zk's grace window both run at the end, inside the container, so neither protects against the platform stopping it.

Recording this rather than editing the earlier note: the original reasoning is worth keeping visible, because 'orphaned' was the plausible-sounding answer and it was reached the same way the seven exit-7 runs were — by inference from an absence, without asking what else produces that absence.

2026-08-27 11:54 - FROM TICK psh — a THREE-way vocabulary contract now held together only by a comment. Phase 2 should cover it.

The collect verdict and status strings are shared by THREE implementations: internal/herd/collect (local), internal/cloud/collect (cloud, laptop side), and cloud/factory/src/worker-collect.ts (the Worker). Until psh landed, the first two were the SAME TYPE by import, so drift between them was impossible by construction. They are now copies.

The failure mode is silent and it is the worst kind: if NEEDS_CONTEXT or ready-to-merge is re-spelled in one place, a cloud run and a herd run disagree about what happened to the same tick and NOTHING FAILS. The report just quietly means something different.

Symbols in the contract: Verdict, ReadyToMerge, NoCommits, MissingResult, BoundaryViolation, StatusBlocked, StatusNeedsContext, ParseStatus.

AND MORE THAN THE CONSTANTS: the statusLine regexp is part of it too — including the DONE_WITH_CONCERNS-before-DONE alternation order (get that wrong and DONE_WITH_CONCERNS parses as DONE, which is a verdict inversion) and the markdown decoration trim set. A fixture that only pins the four constants would miss both.

The psh implementer considered a parity test in internal/herd/collect importing internal/cloud/collect — legal, since the forbidden direction is the other way — and deliberately left it out rather than inverting the dependency in tests. That option is still open and may be cheaper than a full contract artifact for the Go-to-Go half; the Go-to-TS half needs the artifact regardless.

data.reason:
CANCELLED 2026-08-27 on Peter's steer: "don't like the shape of that. let's not overload tk. I want to lean towards the unix philosophy, composable tools with minimum dependencies."

This epic was going to add git-style PATH dispatch to tk, so that an unrecognised 'tk foo' resolved to a tk-foo binary and ticfac could keep owning 'tk factory ...' from outside the binary. It is deleted from the plan, not deferred.

WHY IT WAS WRONG, on both halves of its own reasoning:

1. THE COST I CITED FOR A SEPARATE BINARY WAS NEAR-ZERO AND I OVERSTATED IT. The argument against 'ticfac deploy' was that it "breaks every doc and all muscle memory". Checked against every published tag including v0.31.1: ZERO cmd/tk/cmd/factory* files in any release. tk factory has never shipped. There are no users to break and no installed documentation to invalidate — the habit exists in one working tree.

2. DISPATCH WOULD MAKE TICKS BIGGER IN ORDER TO MAKE IT SMALLER. A PATH resolver, argument and exit-code passthrough, and a suggestion path that still behaves for genuinely unknown commands — all new code in tk, existing solely to serve a product that had just been removed from the repo for being out of scope. Meanwhile the mechanism actually required already exists: init() self-registration with no central registry means deleting a command file removes the command with zero edits elsewhere.

WHAT REPLACES IT: nothing. ticfac is its own binary — ticfac deploy, ticfac run, ticfac status. tk never learns that a factory exists. The composition happens where Unix puts it: two independent programs, one text interface. ticfac runs 'tk ... --json' to read the tracker; tk runs nothing. The dependency points one way.

CONSEQUENCES NOW OWNED BY PHASE 5 (5hm), noted there: the sandbox image installs two binaries rather than one plus a shim, and required-tk-commands splits into two lists each owned by the product that ships it. 'tk cloud ...' becomes 'ticfac ...'; whether 'cloud' survives as a SUBSTRATE NAME in .tick/runners.toml stays a Phase 6 question, and probably yes, since runners.toml already names herdr without ticks owning it.

There is no shim. cloud/sandbox/required-tk-commands SPLITS: 'tk sandbox ...' stays a tk dependency checked against tk; 'cloud branch' becomes a ticfac command checked against ticfac. data.reason:
Completed as a DECISION with the measurement behind it, which was the ask.

MEASURED (go1.26.2, darwin/arm64, cold cache, variants built by moving command files aside and reverted):
- tk as it ships: 22,728,802 bytes
- minus factory_dashboard.go (the edge ffy names): -163,472 B, -0.72%
- minus the whole tk factory command family: -2,069,792 B, -9.1%
- Dependency surface: 4 packages of 337, computed by differencing dep closures — internal/factory, internal/factory/dashboard, crypto/pbkdf2, crypto/internal/fips140/pbkdf2. ZERO third-party modules; cobra, bubbletea and net/http are already in tk for its own commands.
- Compile time: no signal (6.00 / 6.22 / 6.37 s across three cold builds).

DECISION: defer to Phase 5. The 9% column is only reachable by dropping tk factory deploy/setup/status/webhook — that is a different tk, not a cheaper build of the same one — so a build tag actually buys the 0.72% row. Not worth a build-tag scheme.

data.note:
2026-08-28 16:10 - RESHAPED (Peter, 2026-08-28): "should tell/channel live in ticks? ideally ticks have 0 factory couplings."

They should not, and that inverts the phase. My plan an hour ago was to BUILD an outbound endpoint on the factory and point tk tell at it. That would have created a NEW ticks -> factory coupling — precisely the thing the extraction exists to remove — while congratulating itself for deleting an old one.

THE INVERSION, and it needs no new endpoint at all. The CLI surface already exists:
  tk list --awaiting        finds parked questions
  .tick/pending             holds the entries
  tk answer <id> <answer>   resolves one
So ticfac reads parked questions through the tk CLI, delivers them to Telegram, and writes answers back with tk answer. ZERO Go coupling in either direction, and the seam is the CLI — exactly what Phase 1 established. The factory reaches into ticks; ticks never reaches out.

WHAT THAT MEANS FOR internal/operator. The split is not "delete the telegram subpackage" — it is one line further in:
  STAYS: PendingStore, Pending, Question, mapping, the parking half of tk ask, tk answer / approve / reject, .tick/pending. Terminal answering, offline, no factory.
  GOES:  internal/operator/telegram/**, AND the Channel interface with its capability interfaces (Adopter, ContextualChannel, FormattedSender, AttachmentSender), AND Consumer in engine.go. Those are the in-process transport extension point, and the CLI replaces them. A Channel interface with no implementation is not a seam, it is a stub.

AND tk tell / tk channel LEAVE. Not "repoint" — relocate. tell.go already exits 4 without a channel and its only channel is Telegram, so it is entirely a remote-notification feature. channel.go is bot-token pairing for a transport that is leaving.

THE ONE CALL WORTH OVERRIDING, so it is on the record rather than assumed: I do not think tk tell needs to survive anywhere. In a terminal-first ticks an agent that wants to tell you something prints it, and anything needing a response goes through the parked-question mechanism. tell exists to reach you when you are AWAY, which is the cloud feature by definition. If you want an equivalent later it is a ticfac command, not a tk one. Say so if you disagree — it changes what gets deleted rather than moved.

2026-08-31 13:22 - MAPPED BEFORE PLANNING (2026-08-31). Three facts that shape this phase, none of them in the epic's original description.

1. THE FILE IS 88% FACTORY BY KEY COUNT. internal/ticksrc defines FIFTEEN KeyFactory* constants — URL, Token, Version, CloudflareAPIToken, GatewayURL/Provider/Key, GitHubAuth/Login/Repo/Token/TokenExpires/RefreshToken/RefreshExpires, WorkersAIBillingMode — against exactly TWO non-factory ones, KeyToken and KeyURL. This is not a shared file with some factory keys in it. It is a factory credentials file with two board-sync keys still living in it.

2. THERE ARE TWO INDEPENDENT READERS OF THE SAME FILE, and only one of them uses the package. internal/tickboard/cloud/client.go declares its OWN ConfigFileName = ".ticksrc" and its OWN readConfigFile() that parses the file by hand into a two-field struct. It never imports internal/ticksrc. So ~/.ticksrc is parsed twice, by two implementations, in one binary — the exact duplication class this project has been removing everywhere else, and it has no contract holding the two parsers together.

3. TWO CORE COMMANDS READ FACTORY KEYS. cmd/tk/cmd/upgrade.go:69-80 reads KeyFactoryURL and KeyFactoryVersion to warn that a deployed factory is behind. cmd/tk/cmd/board.go reads the file for board sync. upgrade is the surviving ticks->factory coupling that this phase has to answer for; board is the reader that must keep working through whatever split happens.

WHY THIS PHASE IS THE ONE THAT CAN BREAK SOMEONE: those fifteen keys include live GitHub OAuth refresh tokens and a Cloudflare API token on real machines. A cut migrates nothing; a rename strands a deployment. It needs a migration path and evidence that a populated pre-split file still authenticates afterwards.

AND THE REASON IT MATTERS BEYOND TIDINESS: Phase 4b found that tk ask/answer silently read this file and called a deployed Worker. That escape hatch existed BECAUSE factory credentials live somewhere the terminal path could reach. Splitting them is what makes that class of bug impossible rather than merely removed.

data.note:
2026-09-01 10:06 - READINESS CHECK BEFORE PLANNING (2026-09-01). Phase 5 is NOT a file move yet. There is a decoupling tranche first, and it exists because the plan changed underneath Phase 1.

WHAT PHASE 1 ACTUALLY CLEANED: internal/factory/**, internal/cloud/** and internal/gatewaytrace/**. Those are clean — they import only the factory's own packages plus internal/factory/credentials.

WHAT IT DID NOT CLEAN: cmd/tk/cmd/cloud*.go and factory*.go. At the time those were STAYING in ticks, because the plan then had tk dispatching 'tk factory ...' to an external binary. Peter cancelled that on 2026-08-28 — ticfac is its own binary — so those ~23 command files now LEAVE, and every ticks package they import becomes a cross-repo import of an internal/ package, which Go forbids outright.

THE FIVE REMAINING EDGES, all from the command files:
  internal/tick        cloud_test.go, cloud_tk_test.go, cloud_wave_test.go — TESTS ONLY. The tracker. Should become tk CLI calls, the same answer Phase 1 gave for the non-test sites.
  internal/github      cloud.go, cloud_wave.go — copy it, as tick psh already did for internal/factory. Do NOT promote: it handles OAuth device-flow token exchange.
  internal/tui         factory_dashboard.go — shared TUI scaffolding. Copy or let ticfac own its own, same reasoning as the palette decision.
  internal/herd/config cloud_wave.go — reads .tick/runners.toml. NOTE: contracts/runners-config-contract.json now pins that format across languages, so this one has a contract-shaped answer rather than a copy-shaped one.
  internal/sandbox     cloud_branch.go, cloud_inrun.go — and this is the knot the spec already flagged: internal/sandbox STAYS in ticks (herd_spawn uses it), while cloud/sandbox/*.sh moves. The command files that bridge them leave. Decide this deliberately; it is the one edge with no obvious right answer.

SO THE PHASE HAS TWO TRANCHES: cut these five edges while everything is still in one tree and one test run can prove it, THEN move. Same ordering discipline that made Phase 1 and Phase 4b work — do the hard change while both halves are still in one place.

Do not treat this as a defect in Phase 1. Its acceptance was written against the plan of the day and it met it; the plan changed afterwards, which is exactly why this check happened before planning rather than during the move.
